UAE Imposes Temporary Tariffs on Imported Construction Equipment, Impacting Domestic Engineering & Construction Firms

The United Arab Emirates has implemented a new temporary tariff on imported construction equipment and engineering products, sending ripples through the national Engineering & Construction industry. The measure, announced by the Ministry of Economy last week, imposes a 15% tariff on a range of machinery, cranes, and specialized vehicles critical to ongoing and planned projects across the Emirates.

The policy, which took effect immediately, is intended to bolster the local manufacturing of construction equipment and encourage domestic investment, according to government spokesperson Hassan Al-Mansouri. “This tariff is designed to support our national capabilities, reduce reliance on imports, and stimulate innovation within the UAE’s Engineering & Construction sector,” Al-Mansouri stated at a press briefing in Abu Dhabi.

However, industry stakeholders report that the sudden move has created significant challenges for firms relying on imported equipment. Emirates Nuclear Energy Corp is among the major companies affected, with key managers expressing concern about project timelines. “Our current projects require highly specialized machinery, much of which is sourced internationally,” said Fatima Al Suwaidi, engineering director at Emirates Nuclear Energy Corp. “The tariff has forced us to reassess procurement plans and may impact both schedules and budgets.”

Smaller firms such as Al Noor Engineering Services are also feeling the squeeze. “We had several shipments of tower cranes en route when the tariff was announced,” said company CEO Khalid Aziz. “The cost increase has put unexpected pressure on our cash flow, and we’re working to renegotiate with clients.”

The new tariff has led some sites to slow down or temporarily halt non-critical activities while companies revise equipment supply strategies. Workers at several construction sites in Dubai and Abu Dhabi reported reduced overtime hours and a pause in the hiring of additional skilled labor. “Our teams are waiting for new equipment that’s now delayed or more expensive than planned,” said site manager Rami Hassan. “We’re doing our best to keep everyone engaged, but there’s definitely uncertainty.”

Industry analysts estimate that the cost of affected imported equipment has risen by an average of 12% since the tariff’s introduction, with some firms facing higher increases depending on contract terms and inventory levels. The Emirates Engineering & Construction Federation has called for urgent consultations with authorities, warning of potential setbacks to national infrastructure and energy projects if the measure remains in place for an extended period.

As the tariff continues to be enforced, Engineering & Construction firms across the UAE are closely monitoring developments and exploring alternative sourcing and supply chain strategies to mitigate its impact. The Ministry of Economy has not indicated when the temporary measure might be lifted.
